etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English deeth, from Old English dēaþ, from Proto-West Germanic *dauþu, from Proto-Germanic *dauþuz (compare West Frisian dead, Dutch dood, German Tod, Swedish död, Norwegian død), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰówtus. More at die.

quote.citation: 2018 March 30, Chris Buckley, “‘Vicious’ Killer of 11 Women Gets Death Penalty in China”, in The New York Times‎[3], →ISSN, →OCLC, archived from the original on 31 March 2018, Asia Pacific‎[4]:
quote.text: Thirty years after Gao Chengyong embarked on a succession of 11 rape-murders of women in northwest China, a court sentenced him to death on Friday, following an investigation that involved sifting through 230,000 fingerprints.

definitions.definition: The cessation of life and all associated processes; the end of an organism's existence as an entity independent from its environment and its return to an inert, nonliving state.

quote.citation: 1680, T. K., The Kitchin-Phyſician; Or, a Guide for Good-Housewives in Maintaining Their Families in Health.  […] ‎[2], To cure the faintneſs of the Heart, page 71:
quote.text: But foraſmuch as this [the faintneſs of the Heart] is a very bad and heavy diſtemper, and a fore-runner of death, therefore 'tis called a timely death.

quote.citation: 1879, R[ichard] J[efferies], chapter 1, in The Amateur Poacher, London: Smith, Elder, & Co., […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Perhaps the reason why he seemed in such a ghastly rage was that he did not come by his death fairly.

quote.citation: 1900, Charles W. Chesnutt, chapter I, in The House Behind the Cedars:
quote.text: "‘Death,’" quoted Warwick, with whose mood the undertaker's remarks were in tune, "‘is the penalty that all must pay for the crime of living.’"

quote.citation: 2013 July-August, Philip J. Bushnell, “Solvents, Ethanol, Car Crashes & Tolerance”, in American Scientist:
quote.text: Furthermore, this increase in risk is comparable to the risk of death from leukemia after long-term exposure to benzene,  […]

definitions.definition: (often capitalized) The personification of death as a (usually male) hooded figure with a scythe; the Grim Reaper.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Revelation 6:8:
quote.text: And I looked, and behold, a pale horse, & his name that sat on him was Death"

quote.citation: 1762, [Laurence Sterne], chapter IX, in The Life and Opinions of Tristram Shandy, Gentleman, volume V, London:  […]  T. Becket and P. A. Dehondt, […], →OCLC, page 51:
quote.text: [T]o thoſe, Jonathan, who know what death is, and what havock and deſtruction he can make, before a man can well wheel about—'tis like a whole age.

quote.citation: 1974, Anthony Banks, Michael Rutherford, Peter Gabriel, Phil Collins, Steve Hackett (lyrics and music), “Anyway”, in The Lamb Lies Down on Broadway, performed by Genesis:
quote.text: O boy! running man is out of death ... Anyway, they say she comes on a pale horse

definitions.definition: (figuratively, especially followed by of-phrase) A cause of great stress, exhaustion, embarrassment, or another negative condition (for someone).
(preceded by the) The collapse or end of something.

quote.citation: 1983, Robert R. Faulkner, Music on Demand, page 90:
quote.text: He may even find himself being blamed if the project dies a quick and horrible death at the box office or is unceremoniously axed by the network.
